title: Spoked-wheel chariot invented
summary: Herders of the Sintashta culture, in the steppes east of the southern Ural Mountains, bury their dead with light two-wheeled vehicles whose wheels have spokes instead of solid wooden discs. These are the earliest known true chariots: fast, horse-drawn and light enough to carry a driver and a warrior.
significance: Within a few centuries the chariot spread from the steppe to Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, India and China, transforming warfare and the prestige of elites across Eurasia.

title: Assyrian merchants trade at Kanesh
summary: Merchant families from the city of Ashur in northern Mesopotamia run a trading colony at Kanesh in central Anatolia. Donkey caravans carry tin and fine textiles north and bring back silver and gold, and the merchants record their deals in tens of thousands of clay tablets found at the site.
significance: The Kanesh tablets are the earliest large archive of private business letters and contracts, showing long-distance trade, credit and partnerships organized by families rather than kings.

title: Decline of the Indus Valley Civilization
summary: The great planned cities of the Indus Valley, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, are gradually abandoned and people move to smaller villages, many further east. Long-distance trade fades and the Indus script falls out of use. The causes are still debated; shifting monsoon rains and drying rivers are leading explanations, and the old idea of a sudden invasion is no longer accepted.
significance: South Asia's first urban civilization dissolved into rural cultures, and cities would not return to the region on a large scale until the Ganges valley urbanized centuries later.

title: Epic of Gilgamesh written down
summary: Scribes in Babylonia combine older Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, a legendary king of Uruk, into a single long epic in the Akkadian language. It follows Gilgamesh's friendship with the wild man Enkidu and his failed search for immortality. The best-known version is a later edition found in the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.
significance: Often called the oldest great work of literature to survive, it includes a flood story strikingly similar to the one in the Bible and still speaks to readers about friendship and death.

title: Code of Hammurabi
summary: King Hammurabi of Babylon has 282 laws carved on stone pillars set up across his kingdom. The laws cover trade, property, family and crime, with punishments that often depend on the social rank of the people involved.
significance: One of the earliest and most complete written law codes, it established the idea that a ruler publishes fixed laws that apply across a whole state.

title: Andronovo culture spreads across the steppe
summary: Related groups of herders known to archaeologists as the Andronovo culture spread across the steppes from the southern Urals to southern Siberia and Central Asia. They raise cattle, sheep and horses, work bronze and mine copper and tin. Many scholars link them to early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages, though this is debated.
significance: Andronovo herders helped connect the steppe with Central Asia, Iran and northwestern China, spreading horses, chariots and metalworking across a vast area.

title: Kingdom of Kerma at its height
summary: The Nubian kingdom centered on Kerma, in what is now northern Sudan, controls much of the Nile valley south of Egypt. Its capital has a huge mud-brick temple, the Western Deffufa, and its kings are buried in enormous mounds. While Egypt is divided, Kerma's armies raid deep into Egyptian territory.
significance: Kerma was the first great kingdom in Africa south of Egypt, and it showed that Nubia was a power in its own right rather than a mere frontier of Egypt.

title: Minoan palace of Knossos at its height
summary: After an earthquake around 1700 BC, the Minoans of Crete rebuild their palaces on a grander scale. Knossos becomes a sprawling complex of courtyards, storerooms, staircases and colorful wall paintings at the center of a seafaring trade network. The Minoans write in a script called Linear A, which is still undeciphered.
significance: Minoan Crete was one of Europe's earliest advanced civilizations, and its art, palaces and writing strongly influenced the Mycenaean Greeks who followed.

title: Poverty Point earthworks built
summary: In what is now northeastern Louisiana, people who live by hunting, fishing and gathering build six concentric C-shaped earth ridges and several large mounds. The site is used and enlarged for several centuries and draws stone and copper from as far away as the Great Lakes and the Appalachians.
significance: Poverty Point shows that large-scale monumental building did not require farming, and it is one of the largest early earthwork sites in North America.

title: Hittite kingdom founded
summary: King Hattusili I makes the city of Hattusa in central Anatolia his capital and unites much of the region into the Hittite kingdom. He and his successors campaign into northern Syria. The Hittites write on clay tablets in their own language, the oldest written Indo-European language known.
significance: The Hittites became one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age, rivaling Egypt for control of Syria and the Levant for centuries.

title: Mycenaean civilization rises
summary: Warrior elites in mainland Greece begin to bury their dead in deep shaft graves at Mycenae, filled with gold masks, weapons and imported treasures. Over the following centuries they build fortified palaces and record their administration in Linear B, the earliest known written form of Greek.
significance: The Mycenaeans were the first Greek-speaking civilization, and their world became the setting for the later Greek legends of Troy and its heroes.

title: Nebra sky disc made
summary: A bronze disc inlaid with gold shapes of the Sun or Moon, a crescent and stars, including a cluster that looks like the Pleiades, is buried on a hilltop in what is now central Germany. It was found by illegal treasure hunters in 1999. Most researchers date its burial to about 1600 BC.
significance: It is the oldest known concrete depiction of the night sky, suggesting that Bronze Age Europeans tracked the heavens, possibly to help set their farming calendar.

title: Shang dynasty founded
summary: According to tradition, Tang of Shang overthrows the last Xia king and founds a dynasty that rules the Yellow River valley for about 500 years. The Shang build walled cities, cast elaborate bronze vessels and consult their ancestors with oracle bones.
significance: The Shang is the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by archaeology and its own writing, and that script is the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters.

title: Hittites sack Babylon
summary: The Hittite king Mursili I leads a long-distance raid from Anatolia down the Euphrates and sacks Babylon. The raid ends the dynasty of Hammurabi, but the Hittites do not stay. The exact year is uncertain because scholars use competing chronologies for this period.
significance: The power vacuum let the Kassites take over Babylonia and rule it for over four centuries, and the date of the sack anchors much of the chronology of the ancient Near East.

title: Egypt's New Kingdom begins
summary: Ahmose I, a ruler from Thebes in southern Egypt, drives out the Hyksos, foreign kings who had ruled the north, and reunites the country. This begins the New Kingdom, Egypt's most powerful era, when pharaohs build huge temples at Karnak and Luxor and are buried in the Valley of the Kings.
significance: Egypt became an empire that controlled Nubia and much of the Levant, making it a central player in the international politics of the Late Bronze Age.

title: Egypt conquers Kush
summary: Pharaoh Thutmose I leads his army south into Nubia, defeats the Kingdom of Kerma and carves a boundary inscription beyond the Fourth Cataract of the Nile. His successors complete the conquest, and Egypt governs Nubia through a viceroy known as the King's Son of Kush.
significance: Egyptian rule lasted about four centuries and brought Egyptian gods, temples and writing deep into Nubia, shaping the later Kushite kingdoms that would one day conquer Egypt itself.

title: Bronze working at Ban Chiang
summary: Villagers at Ban Chiang in northeastern Thailand cast bronze tools and ornaments and make distinctive pottery painted with red swirls. When bronze first appeared there is disputed: proposed dates range from about 2000 BC to about 1000 BC.
significance: Ban Chiang is a key site for understanding how metalworking came to Southeast Asia, and it showed that the region had its own long Bronze Age tradition.

title: Indo-Aryan migrations into South Asia
summary: Groups speaking early Indo-Aryan languages, the ancestors of Sanskrit, move gradually from Central Asia into the northwest of the Indian subcontinent. Most scholars see this as a slow movement of herders over generations rather than an invasion, supported by evidence from languages and ancient DNA, although the idea remains politically contested in India.
significance: These migrants brought the language and religious traditions of the Vedas, which mixed with local cultures to shape Hinduism and the Indo-Aryan languages spoken by most of South Asia today.

title: Lapita voyagers begin settling the Pacific
summary: A seafaring people known for pottery decorated with stamped patterns, called Lapita by archaeologists, appear in the islands northeast of New Guinea. Over the next few centuries, in outrigger canoes, they sail thousands of kilometers east to Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, islands no human had reached before.
significance: Lapita voyagers were the ancestors of the Polynesians, beginning the settlement of the remote Pacific, the last major region of the world to be reached by people.

title: Rigveda composed
summary: In the Punjab region, poet-priests compose the Rigveda, a collection of more than 1,000 hymns in early Sanskrit addressed to gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna. The hymns are memorized and passed on orally with remarkable precision for many centuries before being written down.
significance: The Rigveda is the oldest text of Hinduism and one of the oldest surviving texts in any Indo-European language, and it is still recited in Hindu rituals today.

title: Hatshepsut becomes pharaoh
summary: When the young Thutmose III comes to the throne, his stepmother Hatshepsut rules for him as regent, and within a few years she is crowned pharaoh in her own right. She reigns for about two decades, sponsoring trade expeditions and great buildings such as her temple at Deir el-Bahari.
significance: Hatshepsut was one of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh, and her peaceful, prosperous reign is one of the best documented of any ancient female ruler.

title: Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt
summary: Hatshepsut sends a fleet down the Red Sea to the Land of Punt, a trading partner most likely on the coast of the Horn of Africa. The ships return with myrrh and frankincense trees, ebony, ivory, gold and live baboons, and the voyage is celebrated in reliefs on her temple at Deir el-Bahari.
significance: The expedition is one of the best-recorded long-distance trading voyages of the ancient world and shows early links between Egypt and the Horn of Africa.

title: Battle of Megiddo
summary: Pharaoh Thutmose III leads his army through a narrow mountain pass to surprise a coalition of Canaanite rulers at Megiddo, in what is now northern Israel. After a seven-month siege the city surrenders. Some scholars date the battle to 1482 BC instead.
significance: It is the first battle recorded in reliable detail, it made Egypt master of the Levant, and the name Megiddo later gave rise to the word Armageddon.

title: Akhenaten's religious revolution
summary: Pharaoh Amenhotep IV renames himself Akhenaten and promotes the worship of the Aten, the disc of the Sun, above all other gods, closing temples of the old gods and building a new capital at Amarna. His art style is unusually naturalistic. After his death, Egypt returns to its traditional religion and his name is erased from monuments.
significance: Akhenaten's cult is often called one of the earliest steps toward monotheism, though scholars debate how far it really went, and the Amarna letters found at his capital reveal the diplomacy of the age.

title: Tutankhamun buried
summary: The young pharaoh Tutankhamun, who restored Egypt's traditional gods after Akhenaten, dies at about 19 and is buried in a small tomb in the Valley of the Kings packed with treasures, including a solid gold coffin and a gold mask. The tomb is hidden and largely forgotten until Howard Carter finds it nearly intact in 1922.
significance: As the only royal tomb of its era found largely intact, it is the richest window into ancient Egyptian royal burial and made Tutankhamun the most famous pharaoh in the modern world.

title: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Pharaoh Ramesses II of Egypt and King Muwatalli II of the Hittites clash at Kadesh, on the Orontes River in Syria, in what may be the largest chariot battle ever fought, with thousands of chariots on each side. Ramesses is nearly caught in an ambush, and the result is a stalemate, although he celebrates it as a great victory on temple walls.
significance: Neither empire could defeat the other, which led them to make peace, and the battle is the best-documented of the ancient world thanks to records from both sides.

title: Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty
summary: Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Hattusili III agree a formal treaty of peace, mutual defense and return of fugitives. Each side keeps its own version: the Egyptian text is carved on temple walls at Karnak, and the Hittite version survives on clay tablets from Hattusa.
significance: It is the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives from both sides, and it ended generations of war between the two greatest powers of the Near East.

title: Oracle bone script, earliest Chinese writing
summary: At the late Shang capital near modern Anyang, diviners for King Wu Ding and his successors carve questions to the ancestors on turtle shells and cattle shoulder blades, then apply heat and read the cracks as answers. These inscriptions, rediscovered around 1899, are the earliest known Chinese writing.
significance: The oracle bone script is the direct ancestor of Chinese characters still in use today, giving Chinese one of the longest continuous writing traditions in the world.

title: Iron working spreads
summary: Iron had been smelted in small amounts for centuries, but around 1200 BC smiths in Anatolia, the Levant and Cyprus begin making it in quantity for tools and weapons. Iron ore is far more common than the copper and tin needed for bronze, which had become harder to obtain as trade broke down.
significance: Cheaper metal tools and weapons spread over the following centuries across Europe, Asia and Africa, giving the Iron Age its name.

title: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a few decades, the interconnected kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean fall apart. The Hittite Empire disintegrates, Mycenaean palaces in Greece are destroyed, trading cities such as Ugarit are burned, and Egypt is weakened. Historians debate the causes, which likely combined drought, earthquakes, raids by the Sea Peoples, rebellions and the breakdown of trade.
significance: It ended the Bronze Age world of palace kingdoms and opened a darker period from which new societies emerged, including the Phoenician cities, Israel and later Greek city-states.

title: Olmec civilization emerges
summary: On the Gulf Coast of Mexico, the Olmecs build San Lorenzo, Mesoamerica's first large ceremonial center, with earthen platforms, drainage systems and colossal stone heads that probably portray their rulers. They trade jade, obsidian and other goods across much of Mexico and Central America.
significance: The Olmecs are often seen as Mesoamerica's first civilization, and their art, ball game and religious ideas influenced later cultures such as the Maya and the peoples of central Mexico.

title: Zoroaster founds Zoroastrianism
summary: The prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) teaches that the world is a struggle between truth and goodness, led by the wise god Ahura Mazda, and the forces of the lie, and that each person must choose a side. His hymns, the Gathas, are in an ancient eastern Iranian language. His dates and homeland are uncertain: many scholars place him between about 1500 and 1000 BC, while others argue for the 6th century BC.
significance: Zoroastrianism became the main religion of the Persian empires, and its ideas of a final judgment, heaven and hell and a cosmic battle of good and evil may have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

title: Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples
summary: Pharaoh Ramesses III defeats a coalition of seaborne raiders, the Sea Peoples, in battles on land and at the mouths of the Nile. He records the victory in reliefs at his temple at Medinet Habu. The origins of the Sea Peoples are still uncertain; one group, the Peleset, is usually identified with the Philistines.
significance: Egypt survived the upheavals that destroyed its neighbors, but the cost weakened it, and defeated groups settled along the coast of Canaan.

title: Phoenician alphabet
summary: Scribes in Phoenician cities such as Byblos use a standardized script of just 22 letters, each standing for a consonant sound, developed from earlier alphabets of the region. It is far easier to learn than the hundreds of signs of cuneiform or hieroglyphs, and Phoenician traders carry it around the Mediterranean.
significance: Adapted by the Greeks, who added vowels, and by the Aramaeans, it became the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic alphabets used by billions of people today.

title: Zhou overthrow the Shang
summary: King Wu of Zhou, from the Wei River valley in the west, defeats the last Shang king at the Battle of Muye, near the Shang capital. The Zhou justify their conquest with the idea that Heaven had withdrawn its mandate from the corrupt Shang. The date 1046 BC comes from a modern Chinese chronology project; other dates have been proposed.
significance: The Zhou became the longest-ruling dynasty in Chinese history, and the Mandate of Heaven became the standard way to explain the rise and fall of Chinese dynasties for 3,000 years.
